in_sanskrit.name: जल्विका
in_sanskrit.long_meaning: वज्रिका (Vajrika) + का (Ka) = Jalvika. Vajrika means 'thunderbolt', and Ka means 'with'. So, Jalvika means 'with thunderbolt'.

in_hindi.name: जल्विका
in_hindi.long_meaning: जल (Jal) means 'water' and विका (Vikā) means 'movement' or 'waves'. So, Jalvika could mean 'waves in water' or 'water in motion'.

data.cultural_impact: The name Jalvika is closely connected to water, an essential element in Indian culture. Water symbolizes purity, nourishment, and life, and is revered in Hinduism as a goddess in her own right (Ganga Mata). The name thus carries a sense of vitality and freshness.
data.spiritual_significance: Jalvika's meaning is deeply tied to the spiritual belief in the power of water. In Hinduism, water is considered sacred, and rivers are thought to be the abode of gods and goddesses. Jalvika evokes the deities of water, and convey a sense of divine presence, grace, and nourishment. The name is believed to bring blessings of prosperity, peace, and strength.

historical_references.reference: Jalvika is mentioned in the ancient Indian epic Mahabharata, as the name of a Yaksha (mythological being) who was the guardian of a lake.
historical_references.context: Mahabharata is an Indian epic that forms a major source of Hindu mythology and Indian literature. It is one of the two major Sanskrit epics of ancient India, the other being the Ramayana. Jalvika, as a Yaksha, is part of the rich mythology surrounding water bodies and their guardians in Hinduism.

historical_references.reference: Another reference to Jalvika is in the 12th century Sanskrit play 'Mrigavadhava' by Kalidasa, where Jalvika is depicted as the name of a king.
historical_references.context: Mrigavadhava is a Sanskrit play by the renowned Indian poet and playwright Kalidasa. It is a tragic tale of a king who is poisoned by his queen and his subsequent interaction with a courtesan named Mrigasena. Jalvika, as a king, is a character in this play and adds to the complex narrative of power, love, and betrayal in ancient Indian literature.
